title: Meissner Technologies: ML-Driven Superconducting Materials for Quantum Computing - News and Statistics
excerpt: Meissner Technologies, founded in 2025 by Olivia Leng, uses machine-learning simulations and lab testing to discover superconducting materials for single-photon detectors, targeting lower cooling costs and a minimum viable photon detector for quantum computing customers.
content:
Oct 28, 2026

Meissner Technologies, a Canadian startup launched in September 2025 by Olivia Leng, a University of Toronto materials science graduate, is addressing a major obstacle to commercializing quantum computing: the superconducting materials employed in single-photon detectors. The company draws on AI, machine-learning simulations, chemical and electrical simulations, and lab testing to uncover new superconducting materials for quantum computing, and it is also investigating materials that might lower the cooling needs of photonic quantum systems.

Most of the Meissner team comes from the University of Toronto. The company has finished the Creative Destruction Lab program, a nonprofit, objectives-driven mentorship initiative for pre-seed and seed-stage deep-tech startups developing massively scalable products and services. Meissner also recently completed its first financing round, led by the BDC Thrive Venture Fund, with support from founders, operators, and investors including Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO of Xanadu.

Leng's route to entrepreneurship started while she was studying, when she worked extensively with superconducting materials in research labs and simulation settings. She noticed considerable momentum behind AI for drug discovery and realized that a comparable framework and approach could be used to find new superconducting materials.

Photonic systems mostly run at room temperature, but they still depend on single-photon detectors that require cooling to extremely low temperatures. Today's detectors generally use niobium titanium nitride or niobium nitride. Leng said these materials create an unavoidable tradeoff between operating temperature and detector performance. Meissner believes improved materials could substantially alter the economics of quantum computing infrastructure.

The company is looking for alternatives that can run a few degrees warmer than current options without sacrificing performance. Although that may seem like a modest gain, Leng contended that the effect could be dramatic. She said that removing dilution refrigerators and replacing them with closed-loop helium-4 cryostats could cut cooling costs by as much as 95 percent.

The problem is growing more pressing because the industry relies on helium-3. Leng noted that constrained global supplies could eventually limit scaling across several quantum computing platforms. She said the company's focus immediately resonated with investors and industry participants, and she described Meissner's goal as becoming the picks and shovels of quantum computing, where she believes a large share of the value chain can be captured.

With new funding in hand, Meissner is shifting from computational discovery to experimental validation. For several months, the company focused on improving its simulation stack. It is now moving promising material candidates into fabrication and testing. Leng said the company deposits them into thin films, etches them into nanowires, packages them into photon detectors, and runs actual lab tests, then feeds that lab data back into its model to create a circular materials discovery pipeline.

The next major milestone is to deliver a minimum viable photon detector that can be piloted with a photonic quantum computing customer. A seed financing round is expected next year, with future investment aimed at scaling detector manufacturing. Beyond that, the company has a more ambitious vision: autonomous materials research. Leng said experimental validation is currently the largest bottleneck, noting that Meissner can produce many candidates computationally but has limited manpower. She added that the company ultimately aims to build self-driving laboratories capable of automating much of the materials discovery workflow.

Leng also views Canada as an increasingly attractive location for building a quantum technology company. She cited support from ecosystems in Toronto, Waterloo, and Sherbrooke, as well as a growing base of talent and investors. She said the ecosystem has advanced to the point where building a company in Canada is far more viable, and that Meissner intends to remain Canadian.

Internationally, Meissner faces established detector suppliers such as ID Quantique and Single Quantum. Leng argued that those firms are mainly improving detector performance through engineering refinements, while Meissner is focused on discovering entirely new materials. She said niobium titanium nitride has been around for decades in academia and that every variation has been exhausted, so the only way to meaningfully improve detector performance is to investigate the materials science itself.

The company's technology roadmap could also extend beyond quantum computing. Leng cited opportunities in quantum communications, aerospace sensing applications, and nuclear fusion, all of which rely on advanced superconducting materials. She said Meissner is ultimately a materials discovery company that will not be limited to quantum computing.
